n: Josiah does not keep the rediscovered book to himself. He summons the leaders of the nation so that everyone can hear it together.

f.g: Senior leaders of clans and towns.

n: The king personally reads the entire book aloud at the temple to everyone, from the least to the most important. God’s word is meant for all, not just the elite.

f.g: Everyone, regardless of age or status.

n: Standing by a temple pillar, Josiah makes a covenant to obey the Lord with all his heart and soul, and the people commit themselves to it as well. Covenant renewal is the heart of the reform.

f.g: Probably one of the two great bronze pillars at the temple entrance, a customary place for royal ceremonies (2 Kings 11:14).

f.w: with all their heart and all their soul

f.g: Agreed to it and committed themselves.

n: Josiah orders all the idol equipment out of the temple and burns it outside the city. He takes the ashes to Bethel, the old center of the northern kingdom’s false worship, to defile it.

f.g: Assistant priests ranking below the high priest.
The Kidron Valley, just east of Jerusalem’s temple mount.

n: He removes the pagan priests whom earlier kings had appointed to burn incense to Baal and to the sun, moon, planets and stars.

f.g: Hebrew kemarim, a word used only for priests of false gods.
Probably the constellations or signs of the zodiac.

n: The Asherah pole Manasseh put in the temple is burned, ground to powder, and scattered on a common graveyard—making it ritually unclean and utterly worthless.

f.w: graves of the children of the people
f.g: The public burial ground of ordinary people.

n: He tears down quarters by the temple used for ritual prostitution connected with Canaanite fertility worship, where women also wove cloth for the Asherah.

f.g: Here meaning male cult prostitutes serving in pagan fertility rites.
Woven coverings or tent hangings for the Asherah image.

n: Josiah shuts down all the local shrines across Judah, from Geba in the north to Beer-sheba in the south, centralizing worship at the temple as Deuteronomy teaches.

f.g: The full length of Judah, north to south.

n: The former shrine priests could not serve at the temple altar, but they were still allowed to share the priests’ food—a mix of discipline and compassion.

f.g: Bread made without yeast, part of the priests’ portion.

n: He desecrates Topheth in the Hinnom Valley, where children had been burned as sacrifices to Molech, so it could never be used that way again.

f.g: Probably “fireplace”; the site of child sacrifice south of Jerusalem.

f.w: valley of the children of Hinnom
f.g: Ge-Hinnom, later “Gehenna,” which became a New Testament word for hell.

n: He removes horse statues or live horses dedicated to the sun god at the temple entrance and burns the sun chariots—symbols of a sun cult borrowed from foreign nations.

f.g: Images used in sun worship, picturing the sun riding across the sky.
A royal court official.

n: Josiah destroys rooftop altars from Ahaz’s time and the altars Manasseh built in the temple courts, throwing their rubble into the Kidron Valley.

f.g: Rooftop altars were often used for star worship (Jeremiah 19:13).

f.w: the altars which Manasseh had made

n: Even shrines that King Solomon had built for his foreign wives’ gods, still standing over three centuries later, are finally defiled.

f.g: A play on the Mount of Olives (“anointing”), renamed “destruction” because of its idol shrines.

f.w: Solomon the king of Israel had builded

n: He smashes images, cuts down Asherah poles, and fills the sites with human bones so they become permanently unclean.

f.g: Contact with the dead made a place ritually unclean (Numbers 19:16).

n: Josiah extends his reform north into former Israelite territory and tears down Jeroboam’s altar at Bethel, the very shrine that had led the northern kingdom into sin.

f.w: Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who made Israel to sin

n: He burns bones from nearby tombs on Bethel’s altar—fulfilling, to the letter, a prophecy made about three hundred years earlier that named Josiah before he was born.

f.w: according to the word of the LORD which the man of God proclaimed

n: Josiah notices a grave marker and learns it belongs to the very prophet from Judah who had foretold these events.

f.g: A monument or grave marker.

f.w: the man of God, which came from Judah

n: Out of respect, Josiah leaves that prophet’s bones untouched, along with those of the old prophet who had asked to be buried beside him.

f.w: the prophet that came out of Samaria

n: He removes the shrine buildings throughout the old northern territory of Samaria, treating them just as he had treated Bethel.

f.g: Towns in the former northern kingdom, by then an Assyrian province weakened by Assyria’s decline.

n: Josiah executes the pagan priests of the northern shrines on their own altars—harsh by modern standards, but following the law’s penalty for leading people into idolatry—and returns to Jerusalem.
With the land cleansed, Josiah commands the whole nation to keep the Passover exactly as the rediscovered book directs—celebrating God’s deliverance from Egypt.
This Passover is described as the greatest since the time of the judges—centuries earlier. Its faithfulness to the law, not just its size, made it remarkable.

f.g: Held; observed.

n: It took place in Josiah’s eighteenth year—the same year the book was found. Discovery, repentance, covenant and celebration all happen in quick succession.
Josiah also removes mediums, spiritists, household idols and every other abomination, all to keep the words of the book Hilkiah found.

f.g: Hebrew teraphim—household idols, sometimes used for divination.

n: The narrator’s highest praise: no king before or after turned to the Lord as fully as Josiah, with heart, soul and might—language that echoes Israel’s great commandment.

f.w: with all his heart, and with all his soul, and with all his might
like unto him was there no king before him

n: Even so, the judgment earned under Manasseh is not canceled. A righteous king could delay but not reverse the consequences of a nation’s deep and lasting rebellion.

f.g: Nevertheless; in spite of this.

f.w: the provocations that Manasseh had provoked him withal

n: The Lord declares that Judah will be exiled as Israel was, and even Jerusalem and the temple will be cast off. Reform at the top had not truly changed the people’s hearts.
The usual closing formula points to fuller royal records about Josiah.

f.w: the rest of the acts of Josiah

n: In 609 BC Pharaoh Necho marched north to help Assyria against rising Babylon. Josiah tried to stop him at Megiddo and was killed—a tragic end for a righteous king.

f.g: Necho II of Egypt (reigned about 610–595 BC).

f.w: went up against the king of Assyria
f.g: Better understood as “went up to the aid of” the king of Assyria, as other sources show.

n: Josiah’s body is brought home and buried, and the people crown his son Jehoahaz. Judah mourned Josiah deeply; Jeremiah wrote laments for him.

f.g: Also called Shallum (Jeremiah 22:11).

f.w: buried him in his own sepulchre

n: Jehoahaz rules only three months.

f.g: A different man from the prophet Jeremiah, who came from Anathoth.

n: Despite his father’s example, Jehoahaz returns to evil.

f.w: according to all that his fathers had done

n: Pharaoh Necho, now in control of the region, imprisons Jehoahaz at his headquarters in Riblah and forces Judah to pay heavy tribute.

f.g: In chains.
A town in Syria on the Orontes River, used as a military base by Egypt and later Babylon.
A talent was a large weight, roughly 75 pounds (34 kg).

n: Necho installs another son of Josiah, Eliakim, as a puppet king, renaming him Jehoiakim to show his power over him. Jehoahaz dies in Egypt.

f.g: Renaming a vassal showed the overlord’s authority; the name means “the LORD raises up.”

f.w: came to Egypt, and died there

n: Jehoiakim pays Egypt by taxing his people heavily, demanding silver and gold from each according to his assessment.

f.g: Demanded and collected by force.

n: Jehoiakim becomes king at twenty-five and reigns eleven years (about 609–598 BC).
He too does evil. The prophet Jeremiah strongly condemned him, and he even burned a scroll of Jeremiah’s prophecies.
